notes.meaning: These craftsmen from the tribe of Judah worked as potters and gardeners in towns near the western foothills. They lived and worked directly for the king, shaping clay and caring for royal estates. Their humble daily work was honored because it was done in service to their ruler.

The family record shifts to Simeon, the second son of Jacob, whose descendants lived next to Judah in the south. Five principal sons are listed here as founders of the tribe's main clans. Minor differences in names compared to earlier lists in Genesis and Numbers reflect common spelling variations in ancient records.

This family line traces the descendants of Shaul down through several generations to a man named Shimei. Shaul's branch became the primary surviving line within the tribe of Simeon. Keeping this list preserved each family's identity across many generations.

Shimei was blessed with a large household of sixteen sons and six daughters. However, the other Simeonite families remained small, so the whole tribe never grew as large as Judah. This fulfilled Jacob's ancient prophecy that Simeon's descendants would be divided and scattered throughout Israel.

Simeon's families lived in thirteen towns in the dry southern territory, including Beersheba and Ziklag. Because Simeon was small and weak, they struggled to hold these towns against hostile neighbors like the Philistines. During the reign of King David, several of these cities were recovered and brought under Judah's direct control.

Five outlying towns and their nearby villages also belonged to Simeon, extending south as far as Baal. Even though their settlements were surrounded by the much larger territory of Judah, they kept their own distinct family records. This registration helped them maintain their identity as a separate tribe.

Thirteen clan leaders are named who stepped forward to guide their families during a time of expansion. Although these men are not mentioned elsewhere in scripture, their family lines were carefully documented. Their leadership paved the way for the tribe to seek new territory.

These named chiefs led family groups that were growing significantly in population. Over time, their households and herds became so large that their original lands could no longer sustain them. This shortage of grazing ground forced them to search outward for new settlements.

The Simeonite leaders guided their people toward a valley near Gedor in search of pasture for their sheep and goats. They found a wide, peaceful, and fertile area formerly occupied by descendants of Ham. Because the land was quiet and spacious, it offered ideal grazing ground for their flocks.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Greek translations read 'Gerar' instead of 'Gedor,' pointing to the fertile grazing lands in the western Philistine plains where the patriarchs once lived.

notes.meaning: During the reign of King Hezekiah, these Simeonite chiefs led an attack against the tent-dwelling Hamites and Meunites in the valley. They completely destroyed the inhabitants and took possession of the land for themselves. This campaign gave the Simeonites a lasting territory with plenty of grazing land.

Another group of five hundred Simeonite men marched southeast into the hill country of Mount Seir. There they defeated the surviving remnant of the Amalekites and settled permanently in their place. This victory brought an end to a longstanding enemy of Israel and provided Simeon with a secure home.
